name: Parthian Empire
summary: An Iranian empire (the Arsacids) that stood between Rome and Han China on the Silk Road. Its horse archers defeated Rome at Carrhae.

location.value: Iran and Mesopotamia, from the Euphrates to Afghanistan.

terrain.value: The Iranian plateau, mountains and the Tigris–Euphrates plain.
terrain.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

climate.value: Mostly arid, with fertile river valleys in Mesopotamia.
climate.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

resources.value: Farmland, horses, and control of trade routes.
resources.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

disasters.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

population.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

urbanisation.value: Ctesiphon on the Tigris became the main capital; Hecatompylos and Ecbatana were earlier or seasonal capitals.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Parthian Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

disease.value: The Antonine Plague may have come from Roman troops in Mesopotamia.
disease.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

migration.value: The Parni, a nomadic tribe, moved into the province of Parthia around 247 BCE.

economicBase.value: Farming and Silk Road trade between Rome and Han China.

tradeRoutes.value: The Silk Road between Rome and Han China.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Parthian Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

moneyAndTax.value: The silver drachma, with the king’s portrait; taxes and tribute from vassals.

inequality.value: The royal Arsacid family and great noble houses held most land.
inequality.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

governmentType.value: Monarchy (“King of Kings”) with many vassal kings.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Parthian Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

keyRulers.value: Arsaces I, Mithridates I (c. 171–132 BCE), Mithridates II (124–91 BCE), Artabanus IV (last).

succession.value: Hereditary within the Arsacid family, often contested.
succession.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

institutions.value: A council of nobles (the Megistanes) and vassal kings.

stability.value: Frequent civil wars between rival Arsacids.
stability.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

eliteConflict.value: Powerful noble clans (such as the Suren and Karen) could make and unmake kings.
eliteConflict.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

majorWars.value: The Battle of Carrhae (53 BCE) against Rome; the Roman–Parthian Wars.

territoryChange.value: Perhaps about 2.8 million km² around 1 CE, from the Euphrates to Afghanistan.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Seleucids, Rome and the Kushans.

inventions.value: The “Baghdad Battery” is sometimes dated to this period, but its purpose is debated.

scienceEducation.value: Little is known; Greek learning continued in cities such as Seleucia.
scienceEducation.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

openness.value: Used Greek, Parthian and Aramaic; tolerated many religions.

communicationTransport.value: Controlled Silk Road caravan routes between Rome and China; mounted messengers.

religion.value: Zoroastrianism, Babylonian religion, Buddhism and others.

languageWriting.value: Parthian at court, written in an Aramaic-based script; Greek and Aramaic also used.

artsArchitecture.value: The iwan (a vaulted hall open at one end).
artsArchitecture.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

socialStructure.value: King, great nobles, vassal kings, townspeople and farmers.
socialStructure.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

sharedIdentity.value: Claimed the Iranian heritage of the Achaemenids.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses with courtyards; bread, rice, dates and wine; trousers and tunics.

neighbours.value: Rome, the Seleucids, the Kushans and Armenia.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism and other religions spread along the Silk Road.
ideasReligions.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

colonisation.value: Ruled through vassal kings in Armenia, Persis, Characene and elsewhere.
colonisation.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

riseSignals.value: Mithridates I greatly expanded the empire.

peakPeriod.value: Under Mithridates II (about 124–91 BCE), who first sent envoys to China.
peakPeriod.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

declineSignals.value: Civil wars, Roman invasions, and a revolt by the Sasanians.
declineSignals.source: Curtis & Stewart (eds), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

outcome.value: Ardashir I defeated Artabanus IV in 224 CE. Successor: the Sasanian Empire.

sources.value: Greek and Roman writers, coins. Checked against Wikipedia (“Parthian Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Medium. Few Parthian sources survive; many dates are uncertain.

knownFor.label: Horse archers
knownFor.note: Mounted archers whose “Parthian shot” defeated Rome at Carrhae.

knownFor.label: The iwan hall
knownFor.note: A vaulted hall that became a feature of Persian and Islamic architecture.
